source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Founding verbal-protocol study of debugging. Professional programmers debugged a COBOL sales-report program with one logic bug, thinking aloud. Protocols were cut into episodes, then strategy diagrams, then a process model.
numbers: N=16 programmers (8 expert, 8 novice) from one state government computer centre. Two program versions: high-level bug (line 299, branch-change flag not reset) and low-level bug (line 308, customer-change flag not reset); 4 experts and 4 novices per version. Subjects first debugged a practice program.
limits: One bug type, one COBOL program, one site, tiny N. Authors call it exploratory and say the expert/novice classifier was never tested for reliability (no test-retest).
agent_relevance: Shows the unit of study for our agent: goal episodes, not final answers. Log each step as a goal (determine, understand, locate, repair, confirm) so code can check order.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Goal hierarchy of debugging. Four strategic goals: (1) determine the problem, (2) gain familiarity with program function and structure, (3) explore program structure and execution/control, (4) repair the error. Repair splits into tactical goals locate error, repair error, confirm error. Tactical goals include compare correct and incorrect outputs, examine listing, mentally process data through program. Operational goals are single episodes (examine next module, explore working-storage item, evaluate problem).
numbers: Goals 1 and 4 appear in every protocol; goals 2 and 3 appear often but with different weight. All 16 protocols fit five building blocks: problem determination, gain familiarity, explore, evaluate (hypothesis), repair.
quote: Strategic goals ... tactical goals that specify how a strategic goal is to be fulfilled
limits: Goal 4 is last 'except when subjects make errors'. Gould (1975) cited: some programmers read source first instead of output; all 16 here compared outputs first.
agent_relevance: This is the direct source of the 'locate before fixing' rule for S5 REVISE. Maps cleanly: determine = read failing output, familiarity = read code, locate, repair, confirm = rerun check.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Model of debugging functions (Fig. 1): find problem, generate hypothesis, evaluate hypothesis, represent code, error repair, confirm error. Chunking ability is measured against this model by three efficiency signs: number of different debugging functions used, reversals to the top 'debug program' function, and changes of program location.
numbers: Predicted: novices show more function changes, more reversals, more location changes than experts.
limits: Chunking is inferred from behaviour (circular risk): the expert label was derived ex post from the same protocols later used to compare experts and novices.
agent_relevance: A counted signal: number of revisits to the same file/module and number of goal reversals can be computed by code as a flailing detector (supports G1: doubt only on a signal).

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Skill (by chunking classification) and bug level together explained most of the variation in total debug time. Novices took longer overall and engaged in more episodes and major phases. Average episode length did not differ by skill or bug level.
numbers: Total debug time R2=0.737 (skill and bug level both significant). Novices more major phases (P=0.003, R2=0.570). Time to discover the error differed only by skill (P=0.005, R2=0.572). Low-level bug took longer than high-level bug for total time.
limits: Ex post classification was built from process data, so the high R2 is partly built in. Manager ex ante rating did worse (paper argues process classification reduced variability).
agent_relevance: Time lost is from number of episodes, not slower steps: the cost to cut is wasted goal switches, not per-step speed.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Novices made significantly more mistakes (wrong repairs presented as the solution). All programmers who made a mistake were classified novices.
numbers: Mistakes: novices > experts, P=0.005, R2=0.500. 8 mistakes in total; 6 of 8 on the low-level bug. 4 of 8 involved moving SPACES to DETAIL-LINE, 4 involved resetting branch/salesperson/customer numbers.
limits: Counts are very small (8 mistakes). Bug level had no significant effect on mistakes.
agent_relevance: Wrong repairs come from fixing without having located; supports requiring a located cause (G2) before an edit is accepted.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Experts did NOT make better or more first guesses. Novices stated more hypotheses. The key difference was commitment: experts were not as committed to hypotheses and stayed open to new information.
numbers: Hypotheses stated by 9 subjects, 1 to 3 each, 19 hypotheses total (3 control break, 5 reset previous numbers, 9 clear DETAIL-LINE, 2 reset change flag). Novices > experts P=0.045, R2=0.230. Only one subject (an expert) explicitly named the true cause (change flag).
quote: The crucial factor in debugging performance is that experts were not as committed to their hypotheses as novices.
limits: Contradicts the common claim that experts make better first guesses. Tiny N; explicit statement may miss implicit hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Quality of the first guess is not the lever; keeping hypotheses revisable is. Do not reward early confident diagnosis. Fits G1/G2: hold any hypothesis until a check supports it.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Constrained vs unconstrained subjects. Four novices stated a hypothesis early and held to it, failing to understand structure or test their change (NH1, NL2, NL3, NL4). Two novices (NL2, NL3) used shotgun debugging: repeated edits hoping one works, leaving accept/reject to the experimenter.
numbers: Constrained: NH1, NL2, NL3, NL4 (all novices). Unconstrained: EH1, EH3, NH2, NH4. Shotgun: NL2, NL3.
limits: Qualitative classification by the author; no inter-rater reliability reported.
agent_relevance: Shotgun editing is a failure pattern LLM agents also show. A code gate that blocks a new edit unless the previous edit's test result is cited prevents it.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: System thinking. Experts built an implicit model of program structure and function that placed the error in context. Even subjects who found the error quickly had to build the model before they were satisfied. A subject who took twice as long to build the model as to name the error was counted as lacking system thinking.
numbers: Subjects not seen as system thinkers: NL1, NH3, NH4. Number of different modules examined: experts more, P=0.045 (low N). Times module B000 (the faulty module) examined: novices > experts, and low-level bug > high-level bug (P=0.023, R2=0.578).
limits: Based on the Johnson et al. (1982) notion of system thinking from medical diagnosis; Vessey found no support for formal symptom-pattern recognition as in medicine.
agent_relevance: Before fixing, the agent should write a short model of how the code path works (function and structure). The model also serves as a check on the claimed cause.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Strategy propositions (to be tested): experts use breadth-first search with a system view and smooth flow; novices use depth-first search (precautionary vs extraction in Feltovich/Nilsson terms), are weaker at system thinking and show erratic flow. Experts preferred to read the program relaxed before solving; novices rushed to a solution.
numbers: Strategy paths defined by four binary factors (16 possible paths): program vs output first, active vs passive examination, constrained by hypothesis or not, system view or not. Ex post classification and strategy-path classification agreed for all but one subject (NH2).
limits: Abstract says novices were breadth-first but deficient in system thinking and also depth-first; the paper itself notes this tension. Only propositions, not tests. Not replicated in this paper.
agent_relevance: Supports a breadth-first first pass (list several candidate locations, rank by evidence) before depth-first digging.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Limitation and honest status. The study is exploratory with one task. The expertise measure was derived from the same data, and its reliability was untested. Directed search (checking output first, or guessing the module in error) was not a determinant of expertise.
numbers: Comparison with manager rating: author argues the process-based classification reduced variability in debug time and mistakes more than manager assessment.
limits: Later work (Gugerty and Olson 1986/87, Katz and Anderson 1987) partly supports and partly qualifies these propositions; see lines below.
agent_relevance: Treat Vessey's strategy claims as hypotheses, not facts, in the schema evidence table: mark [S].

source: Gugerty and Olson (1986/87) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers
finding: Two experiments with Pascal and LOGO programmers. Experts debugged faster and more accurately than novices and generated correct hypotheses sooner; they did this through better program comprehension. Novices often added new bugs while trying to fix.
numbers: Details (error counts, times) not read. Secondary summary only.
limits: Page was blocked (403); finding taken from search summaries. Treat numbers as unchecked. 1987 HCI 3(4) version exists.
agent_relevance: Replicates the direction of Vessey (experts faster, fewer new bugs) with a different method; pairs with the understand-before-fix idea.

source: Katz and Anderson (1987) Debugging: an analysis of bug-location strategies
finding: Four experiments on LISP debugging by students. Students usually fixed the bug once they found it; the hard part was locating it. Strategy choice differed for own programs and other people's programs.
numbers: Page failed to load; only the search summary was read. No numbers confirmed.
limits: Not opened; claims second-hand.
agent_relevance: Supports the S5 split: location is the bottleneck, repair is easy once located. Matches Olausson (feedback quality is the bottleneck) below.

source: Boehme et al. (2017) Where is the bug and how is it fixed? An experiment with practitioners (DbgBench), as summarised by Beller et al. (2018)
finding: 12 professional software engineers debugged real C errors; they diagnosed bugs in a remarkably similar way, fault localisation was hard when the error came from several statements together, and submitted patches were plausible but only 58% were correct.
numbers: 12 engineers; 58% of patches correct (as reported in Beller et al.). FSE17 PDF itself returned empty; DbgBench has 27 real C errors.
limits: Second-hand through a citing paper. Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Even trained humans fix wrongly 42% of the time; so a passing check on held-out tests (G3) is needed, not just a plausible patch.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Controlled study of a ranked statement list (Tarantula) in Eclipse. The tool helped only high performers on the easy task. It did not help on the harder task.
numbers: Main experiment 24 students (groups A tool vs B no tool); follow-up 10 students (groups C, D); first pilot 34. Tetris: A 12:42 vs B 14:14 min (not significant overall). NanoXML: A 22:30 vs B 20:16 (not significant). High performers (N=10) Tetris: 8:51 with tool vs 14:28 without (p<0.05). Completion: 18 finished Tetris vs 10 NanoXML. 30 min limit per task.
limits: Students not professionals; two tasks only; a flaw in the first NanoXML ranking forced a rerun. Later studies on professionals report different effects.
agent_relevance: Showing a suspicious location is not enough. The agent needs a located cause plus context, and should not assume a candidate list will be read in order.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Two assumptions of fault-localisation research failed. (1) Programmers do not go down a ranked list one by one. (2) Finding the faulty line does not mean understanding it (no perfect bug understanding).
numbers: Group D (faulty-line rank worsened for Tetris, improved for NanoXML) performed the same as group C: average fraction completed .79 in both. Of 10 participants who clicked the faulty line, only 1 stopped; on average they kept using the tool 10 more minutes, about 61% of their time after first seeing the fault. Jumps skipped about 10 positions on average.
quote: Only 1 participant out of 10 stopped using the tool after clicking on the fault.
limits: Small N (10 usable). Rank manipulation null result may be due to using nearby statements as starting points.
agent_relevance: Locating and verifying are different steps. After locating, the agent should still run a confirm check (Vessey's confirm goal) rather than stop at found-it.

source: Beller, Spruit, Spinellis and Zaidman (2018) On the dichotomy of debugging behavior among programmers (ICSE)
finding: Field data on how developers actually debug. IDE debuggers are rarely used; print statements and logs are common. Debugging is a small share of in-IDE time and experience has little effect on debugger use.
numbers: Survey 176 developers; 458 developers observed with WatchDog (132 with usable data, 18,156 hours). Debugger not run in 91% of IDE sessions. Debugging 13.7% of active IDE time (under 14%). 81.3% use IDE debugging tools per survey, 72.2% examine logs, 71.6% use print statements. SR6: experience has limited to no impact on IDE debugger use.
limits: Only IDE debugging inside Eclipse and IntelliJ is observed; command-line and browser debugging missed. Self-report survey bias.
agent_relevance: Human strategy in the wild is mostly cheap observation (print/log/tests) rather than formal tools. An agent should prefer cheap instrumentation that produces real output (supports G2).

source: Beller, Spruit, Spinellis and Zaidman (2018) On the dichotomy of debugging behavior among programmers (ICSE)
finding: Before debugging intervals, developers were mostly reading or typing code and rarely running tests.
numbers: Events preceding debug intervals: running unit tests 46 (0.5%), other debug intervals 119 (1.2%), reading 4,991 (51.9%), typing 1,802 (18.7%).
limits: Observational; no outcome measure of success.
agent_relevance: Reproduce-then-observe is not the human default; an agent that always reproduces first is already more systematic than average practice.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging reinvented: asking and answering why and why not questions (Whyline)
finding: Developers' hypotheses about causes are mostly wrong at first, and tools that let them ask why did / why didn't about observed output speed location. Control participants searched text for the word color and followed data dependencies by hand.
numbers: Cited: initial guesses wrong almost 90% of the time. Pilot study: Whyline participants median 4 min (range 1 to 12) vs control median 10 min (range 3 to 38), p<.05 Wilcoxon; more than twice as fast as experts without the Whyline, though most Whyline users were self-described novices. Control searches for color returned 62 matches in 9 files. Crystal: 30% more tasks, 20% faster (cited). Alice Whyline: factor of 8 (cited).
quote: developers' initial guesses were wrong almost 90% of the time
limits: Small pilot; novices vs experts confounded with tool.
agent_relevance: Backs the idea that observed output (a failing trace or value) should drive hypotheses, not the agent's guess. Initial guess wrong ~90%: do not trust the first diagnosis.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging reinvented: asking and answering why and why not questions (Whyline)
finding: Tool support for tracing output back to causes moved time-to-locate from long, high-variance search to short, low-variance search.
numbers: Control group 3 to 38 min vs Whyline 1 to 12 min on the same RGB-slider bug; variation in control times was largely due to their strategies (text search vs manual dependency following).
limits: Single bug task in a Java paint app; generalisation to other bugs untested.
agent_relevance: Variation among strategies dominates: a fixed locate procedure reduces variance as well as the mean.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR)
finding: Without external feedback, LLMs do not improve (and often get worse) when asked to review and fix their own answer. With oracle labels telling when to stop, self-correction appears to work, which is a leak.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7 (5 calls), CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (3 calls) then 41.8, HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0, HotpotQA 49.0 to 43.0. Oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CSQA 75.8 to 89.7; GPT-4 HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; changes go correct-to-wrong more than wrong-to-correct.
limits: Reasoning tasks, not code with test execution. Some prompts were criticised as poorly worded.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G2: revise only from real output. A model asked to check its work without a failing signal is as likely to hurt as help.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation? (ICLR)
finding: Self-repair gains are modest once the cost of repair is counted; the bottleneck is the quality of the model's own feedback on why code failed (diagnosis = locating), not rewriting.
numbers: Stronger feedback model lifts weaker coder on APPS and HumanEval. Human feedback study: 16 participants wrote feedback for 40 failing GPT-4 programs (2 each). Repair success with GPT-4's own explanations 33.30% overall (42.64% introductory, 19.33% interview, 3.67% competition) vs human feedback 52.60% overall (62.21%, 45.67%, 14.67%). On APPS only GPT-4 benefits significantly from self-repair; Code Llama and GPT-3.5 match or lag baselines.
limits: Pass@k budgeted comparison; human feedback written by volunteers (n=16) for 40 programs; feedback is free text.
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM match to Katz and Anderson: finding the bug is hard, fixing is easy. Put effort in the locate step (S5), and use real execution output as the feedback source.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching large language models to self-debug (ICLR)
finding: Self-Debugging: the model runs its code, explains it line by line (rubber duck), reads unit-test results, and revises. Execution feedback helps more than explanation alone. Reused failed attempts raise sample efficiency.
numbers: Spider (no unit tests): +2 to 3% with code explanation, +9% on hardest level. TransCoder and MBPP with unit tests: up to +12%. Matches or beats baselines that sample over 10 times more programs.
limits: Gains depend on available unit tests; explanation-only gains are small. Few-shot prompts, specific models.
agent_relevance: The rubber-duck step helps mostly when tied to execution results. Supports G2 and G3: use test output as the signal for revision.

source: Zhong, Wang and Shang (2024) Debug like a human: LDB (ACL Findings)
finding: LDB shows the model the values of variables after each basic block and asks it to verify each block against the task. It imitates a human setting breakpoints, which is a form of locate-by-narrowing.
numbers: Gains up to 9.8% over baseline across HumanEval, MBPP, TransCoder. Table 2 (GPT-3.5 debugger on HumanEval): GPT-3.5 seed 73.8 to Self-Debug 81.1 (+7.3) vs LDB 82.9 (+9.1); GPT-4 seed 87.2 to SD 88.4 vs LDB 89.6; Reflexion seed 91.5 to SD 92.1 vs LDB 95.1. Self-Debugging (+Expl./+Trace) failed to improve StarCoder seeds.
limits: Gains over Self-Debugging are small (1 to 3 points) and benchmarks are saturated; no statistical test.
agent_relevance: Narrowing location by block-level execution state is the machine analogue of Vessey's mentally process data through program. Cheap to run by code.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench: evaluating debugging capability of LLMs (ACL Findings)
finding: 4,253 bug instances in C++, Java, Python, four categories (syntax, reference, logic, multiple). Models are better at fixing syntax errors than logic and multiple bugs. Closed models are below human debuggers.
numbers: Per-type pass rates (e.g. misused ==/=: gpt-4 87.9, gpt-3.5 70.5, human 11/12; logic operation error: gpt-4 68.6, gpt-3.5 49.5, human 10/12; triple bugs: gpt-4 58.9, human 9/12). Fixing syntax and reference errors is easier than generating code; logic or multiple bugs are as hard as writing the code. Phi correlation of debug and code pass rates 0.1 to 0.3.
limits: Bugs are implanted by GPT-4 into LeetCode solutions; authors argue realism with win-rate tests; leakage risk acknowledged.
agent_relevance: Hard bugs are the ones needing real localisation; syntax-level gains do not transfer.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench: evaluating debugging capability of LLMs (ACL Findings)
finding: Runtime feedback is a two-edged tool. Traceback info helps locate syntax and reference errors but is often too low-level for logic bugs and can disrupt the model.
numbers: Figure 4: traceback clearly helps syntax and reference bugs; for logic bugs it may harm. More sampling gives better debugging (cost: tokens), up to nine samples for logic errors.
limits: Effect sizes only in figures; single model for the feedback test (gpt-4-0613).
agent_relevance: Which feedback to show should depend on bug type, and the code can decide from the error type. Raw tracebacks are not always the right signal.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: A fixed three-phase pipeline (hierarchical localise to file, then class/function, then line; repair by multiple candidate patches; validate by tests) beat open-ended agents on SWE-bench Lite at low cost.
numbers: 32.00% (96 of 300 problems) solved at $0.70 average, highest among open-source then. Manual audit of SWE-bench Lite: 4.3% have the exact patch in the issue text, 10.0% miss critical information, 5.0% contain misleading solutions.
limits: Benchmark issues noted by the authors (leakage). Results are for GPT-4o era models and Python repos only.
agent_relevance: Hard-coded locate-then-fix beats freeform agency. This supports putting locate before fix in code, not leaving it to the model.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: Correct edit location correlates with solve rate across tools, but good file-level location alone is not enough; the fix must also be right.
numbers: Percentage of patches with correct locations correlates heavily with solve rate (Table 1, line/function/file levels). OpenCSG StarShip: 90.0% file-level match yet 23.67% resolved.
limits: Commercial tool; no trajectories to explain the gap. Fixing in a different location may also be valid.
agent_relevance: Report localisation accuracy separately from fix accuracy when measuring the S5 step in our harness.

source: Kang, An and Yoo (2024) A quantitative and qualitative evaluation of LLM-based explainable fault localization (AutoFL)
finding: AutoFL lets an LLM navigate a repo with function calls and return a fault location plus an explanation. Repeated runs give a confidence estimate that reduces false positives. Developers liked a few high-quality explanations over many.
numbers: 798 real bugs (Defects4J Java, BugsInPy Python). Method-level acc@1 up 19.7% over Ochiai on Defects4J and 166.7% on BugsInPy (GPT-3.5); up to 233.3% on BugsInPy with GPT-4. Cites Boehme et al.: bug diagnosis took 66% of debugging time in the human study.
limits: Data-leak risk for Defects4J acknowledged; small developer interview study.
agent_relevance: Repeating locate runs and using agreement as a confidence hint is consistent with G4 only as a hint, not as proof.

source: Adnan and Kuhn (2025) The Debugging Decay Index
finding: Iterative LLM debugging follows an exponential decay in effectiveness. Most models lose 60 to 80% of their debugging effectiveness within 2 or 3 attempts. A strategic fresh start (restart from scratch at planned points) rescues some performance.
numbers: phi4:14b E0 = 83.537% vs phi4-reasoning:14b E0 = 59.146%. Fresh start raised deepseek-coder-v2:16b baseline accuracy from 84.1% to 92.1% and another model from 72.56% to 82.82%.
limits: Preprint, small open models plus one closed; the fresh-start timing was tuned on the same data. Not peer reviewed in the version read.
agent_relevance: Supports an impasse rule: after N failed repairs, code resets context (G1: signal-driven). Matches Vessey's novices stuck on one hypothesis.

source: Yu et al. (2025) OrcaLoca: an LLM agent framework for software issue localization (ICML)
finding: Localisation is a bottleneck for issue-resolving agents. Priority-queue scheduling of search actions, relevance scoring and context pruning raised function-match accuracy.
numbers: On the SWE-bench Lite leaderboard, mean function-match 53.5% and mean resolved rate 33.1%. OrcaLoca: 65.33% function match (open-source SOTA), +6.33 points resolved rate when integrated into an open-source framework. SWE-bench average repo 3,010 files, 438K lines.
limits: Leaderboard means mix systems and dates; only one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Locate quality bounds repair quality; our S5 gate should measure it separately.

source: Meng et al. (2025) LLM-based agents for automated bug fixing: how far are we?
finding: Analysis of six systems on SWE-bench Verified. Symbol-level fault localisation matters more than file or line level; issue text quality matters; incorrect bug reproductions can derail the whole process.
numbers: Top system Emergent E1 solved 64.6% of 500 cases. W&B Programmer improved 25.5% and 28.6% over a weaker system on two localisation measures (file/symbol, as stated in text). Reproduction scripts produced in 70.1 to 80.4% of sampled cases by system.
limits: Systems are closed; numbers are reported as relative percentages; exact table values not all read.
agent_relevance: Reproduce-and-confirm is a real step in modern agents; check the reproduction itself (G3: independent check).
